card.name: Kara Jorga
card.era: Traditional pre-Islamic pastoral origin; revived/popularized in the 2000s-2010s
card.tagline: Lively Kazakh dance miming the gait of an ambling horse
card.profile: Kara Jorga (Kazakh: Qara jorga, 'Black Ambler') is a traditional Kazakh dance and instrumental kuy depicting a horse using an ambling gait, connected to animalistic symbolism and Tengrianism (Wikipedia). Performers imitate a horseman prancing on a pacer through rhythmic leg kicks, springy bounces and swaying shoulders (Central Asia Program). During the Soviet period it was nearly lost amid famine and collectivization, but was preserved by Kazakhs who fled to China, and choreographers Dauren Abirov, Aubakir Ismailov and Sara Zhienkulova staged it as professional choreographic art (Wikipedia). It became popular again in Kazakhstan in the 2000s with rising national identity (Wikipedia).
card.insight: Researchers note Kara Jorga is also called 'buwin biyi' (dance of joints); per Guinness World Records, the largest Kara-Zhorga dance was achieved by 399 participants at an event organised by KazBrand in Astana on 16 December 2011, and the dance was nominated for the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage lists in 2013 (Guinness World Records; Wikipedia).
